html:
A book painted around 1541 by Indigenous artists in Mexico City for the Spanish authorities, probably at the request of the viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, after whom it is named. It uses traditional Aztec picture writing, with notes and explanations added in Spanish.

It has three parts:

  • a history of the Mexica rulers from the founding of Tenochtitlan and the towns each one conquered
  • a list of the tribute each province paid: cloth, cacao, feathers, warriors' costumes, maize and more
  • scenes of daily life, from the naming of a baby and the schooling of boys to marriage and punishments

The codex was meant for the emperor Charles V, but the ship carrying it was taken by French privateers. It passed to the French royal cosmographer, then to England, and is now in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. It remains one of the best sources on how the Aztec state worked.
